pages.why: In one week, a fund analyst reads results from a retailer, a bank and a software company. The retailer leads with same-store sales, the bank with its interest margin and bad loans, the software firm with recurring revenue, and none puts EBITDA on page one. A system that knows only one template will hunt for numbers that are not there and miss the ones that matter.
pages.idea:
Ratios tell you how a business performed. Business quality asks why, and whether it will last.

**Unit economics** looks at one unit: one cup, one café, one customer. A cup sold for ₹200 that needs ₹80 of beans, milk and packaging contributes ₹120 towards rent and salaries. If each unit makes money, growth adds profit; if not, growth adds losses.

Costs are variable, moving with sales (beans, cups), or fixed (rent, salaried staff). **Operating leverage** is the effect of fixed costs: once they are covered, most of each extra sale becomes profit, so profit swings more than sales, in both directions.

**Pricing power** is the ability to raise prices without losing customers. It shows when input costs rise and gross margins hold.

Each sector also has its own language. Recognise these; you need not master them.

- Lenders: **net interest margin** (interest earned minus interest paid, as a share of loans), bad loans (non-performing assets in India) and capital adequacy (the capital a bank holds against its risks).
- Software: **annual recurring revenue** (the yearly value of subscriptions in force), churn (the share of customers lost each year), net revenue retention (what last year's customers pay now, as a percentage of what they paid then), and CAC and LTV (customer acquisition cost and lifetime value: what it costs to win a customer, and what one is worth over time).
- Retail and restaurants: **same-store sales growth** (growth at stores open in both periods).
- Manufacturing: capacity utilisation (output as a share of what the plants can make).
- Real estate: pre-sales (the value of homes booked) and collections (the cash received).

example.text:
Assume Brew Lane's cost of goods sold moves in step with sales, while its operating expenses and depreciation stay fixed for the year. What if FY26 sales had been 10% higher?

{table}

Sales rise 10%, yet EBIT rises from 15 to 21, or 40%. The extra ₹10 crore of sales brings ₹4 crore of extra cost of goods sold, and the other ₹6 crore reaches EBIT, because rent, salaries and depreciation do not change.

40% ÷ 10% = 4: each 1% change in sales moves EBIT by about 4%. That works in reverse too, which is why high fixed costs make a business riskier in a downturn.

Real costs are rarely all fixed or all variable, so treat this as a sketch, not a forecast.

table.caption: ₹ crore, FY26 and with sales 10% higher (assumed)

terms.definition: Revenue and costs for a single unit, such as one cup, café or customer, to show whether each one makes money.
How strongly operating profit responds to a change in sales. High fixed costs make profit swing more than sales, up and down.
terms.formula: % change in EBIT ÷ % change in revenue

terms.definition: The ability to raise prices without losing many customers, seen in gross margins that hold when input costs rise.
A lender's interest earned minus interest paid, as a percentage of the loans and other assets that earn interest.
terms.formula: (Interest earned − interest paid) ÷ average interest-earning assets × 100

terms.definition: The yearly value of the subscription contracts in force today. A snapshot of contracts, not revenue already earned.
Sales growth at stores open in both periods, leaving out new openings and closures.

pages.builder:
Most extraction templates assume a company like Brew Lane: revenue, cost of goods sold, EBITDA, working capital. A bank breaks all of them. Its revenue is mostly interest earned, the interest it pays is its main cost, and its loans are what it sells. Ask a generic template for a bank's EBITDA and it will fail or, worse, return a number that means nothing. A software firm's key figure, annual recurring revenue, is not in the income statement at all; it sits in the investor presentation.

So schemas and metric dictionaries must be sector-aware: each sector gets its own fields, definitions and likely sources.

**Check worth building:** tag every company with its sector, and refuse to compute any metric not defined for that sector, such as EBITDA for a bank.

client.say: We'd build a metric dictionary for each sector you cover, so a bank is never forced into a café chain's template.
client.ask: Which sectors do you cover, and which ones do your templates fit badly?

quiz.prompt: Two café chains each grow sales by 10%. Chain A pays a fixed rent on long leases. Chain B pays rent as a fixed share of its sales. If everything else is the same, whose operating profit rises faster?
options: Both rise by 10%, since their sales grew by the same amount
A's, because its rent stays flat while its sales rise
B's, because its rent falls as a share of its sales
B's, because its rent is lower when sales are weak
quiz.explain: A's rent is fixed, so the extra sales reach profit after only variable costs, and its operating profit grows faster than 10%: that is operating leverage. 'Both rise 10%' is tempting, but profit grows in line with sales only when every cost moves with sales.

quiz.prompt: A café chain's total sales grew 30%, but its same-store sales growth was 2%. What does that tell you?
options: Existing cafés grew 30%, while new cafés grew 2%
Prices across the chain must have fallen by about 28%
Most of the growth came from new cafés, not existing ones
One figure is wrong, since the two cannot differ this much
quiz.explain: Same-store sales growth counts only cafés open in both years, so 2% there against 30% overall means new cafés drove nearly all the growth. Reading 30% as the existing cafés' growth is tempting, but it swaps the two figures: the same-store number is the existing cafés' growth.

quiz.prompt: Assume, as in the lesson, that Brew Lane's cost of goods sold moves with sales, while operating expenses and depreciation are fixed. If FY26 sales had been 20% lower, what would EBIT have been?
quiz.explain: Sales of 80, less cost of goods sold of 32, operating expenses of 40 and depreciation of 5, leave ₹3 crore: an 80% fall in EBIT from a 20% fall in sales. ₹12 crore is the common slip: it cuts EBIT by 20%, as if every cost moved with sales.

quiz.prompt: A small lender's only interest-earning assets are loans averaging ₹100 crore over the year. It earns ₹12 crore of interest on them and pays ₹7 crore of interest on its own borrowings. What is its net interest margin?
quiz.explain: Net interest margin = (12 − 7) ÷ 100 = 5%. 12% is the tempting pick, but that is the yield on loans before the interest the lender pays for its own funding.

quiz.prompt: A credit fund analyst asks, 'Can you reuse the template you built for our consumer companies on our banks and software firms?' Which reply is best?
options: Yes: one template keeps every company comparable, so we can start today.
No, each company needs its own template, built from scratch.
Yes, and we'll compute EBITDA for the banks too, so the sectors line up.
Partly. Which metrics does your team track for banks and software?
quiz.explain: Banks and software firms need their own metrics, so asking which ones the team tracks is how the template becomes sector-aware. Reusing one template is tempting because it looks consistent, but it forces a bank into fields like EBITDA that mean nothing for it.

quiz.prompt: Your system fills a standard template for a bank and reports 'EBITDA margin: 62%'. What went wrong, and which check would catch it?
options: A non-bank template was used; block metrics not defined for the sector
The bank's interest was misread; re-extract it and recompute the margin
No margin can be that high; flag any margin above 50% for review
Banks define EBITDA their own way; ask the model for this bank's
quiz.explain: For a bank, interest paid is the main cost of doing business, so an EBITDA that adds it back means nothing; tagging the sector and blocking undefined metrics stops it being computed. A 50% threshold is tempting, but it would flag healthy software firms and still pass a meaningless bank 'EBITDA' of 30%.

speak.prompt: In 30 seconds, explain to a new colleague why Brew Lane's profit would swing more than its sales.
speak.modelAnswer: More than half of Brew Lane's costs don't move with sales. Rent, salaries and depreciation stay roughly the same whether a café sells a hundred cups or a hundred and ten. So once the ingredients are paid for, most of each extra sale drops to profit. If sales rose 10% and only cost of goods sold rose with them, EBIT would go from 15 crore to 21, up 40%. That's operating leverage, and it cuts both ways: a bad year hits profit much harder than sales.
